draft.answer: No. The conclusion that √2 is rational is false. The parity argument is a contradiction proof: if √2 were rational, choose a representation with least positive denominator; then a²=2b² forces both a and b even, producing a representation with a smaller positive denominator. Thus √2 is irrational. This revised draft supplies the previously missing reduction-to-lowest-terms argument via the well-ordering principle.

approaches.description: Assume √2 is rational, choose an integer representation with least positive denominator, and use parity to contradict that minimality.

proof_steps.justification: By the definition of rational, √2=p/q for integers p,q with q≠0. If q<0, replace p,q by -p,-q; the denominator is then positive.
proof_steps.statement: There is at least one representation √2=a/b with integers a,b and b>0.

proof_steps.justification: Apply the well-ordering principle to the nonempty set of positive integer denominators occurring in representations of √2.
proof_steps.statement: Choose a representation √2=a/b whose positive denominator b is least.

proof_steps.justification: Square √2=a/b to obtain 2=a²/b². Since b>0, multiplying by b² gives a²=2b².
The equation makes a² even. If a were odd, a=2k+1 for an integer k, and a²=4k²+4k+1=2(2k²+2k)+1, which is odd. Hence a is even.
Substitute a=2k into a²=2b²: 4k²=2b², hence b²=2k².
If b were odd, writing b=2l+1 would give b²=2(2l²+2l)+1, which is odd, contrary to step-b-square-even.
With a=2k and b=2l, √2=a/b=(2k)/(2l)=k/l. Since b=2l>0, l>0, and l=b/2<b.
proof_steps.statement: √2 has a positive-denominator representation with denominator smaller than b.

packet.question: A proof claims that sqrt(2) is rational: write sqrt(2)=a/b in lowest terms, square to get a^2=2b^2, and conclude that a and b are both even. Is the proof valid? Assess the conclusion and justify your answer.
